desc:
Many different subsequences of nums can share the maximum possible length among strictly increasing subsequences. Among all of them, return the one that is smallest when compared as a list of values from left to right (compare the first values; if equal, the second values; and so on). All the candidates have the same length, so there are no prefix ties.

Return that subsequence as an array of values. For nums = [10, 9, 2, 5, 3, 7, 101, 18] the longest strictly increasing subsequences have length 4, and the smallest of them is [2, 3, 7, 18].
hints: First find the length L of the longest strictly increasing subsequence. Then think about which first elements can start a subsequence of length exactly L.

Compute f[i], the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence that starts at index i (run LIS on the reversed array with negated values). An element may be chosen at step t only if f[i] equals the number of elements still to choose.

Build the answer greedily: for the remaining count c, among indices after the last chosen index, with f[i] == c and value greater than the last chosen value, take the smallest value (the earliest index among equal values). Group the indices by f to keep the total work linear.
editorial: Let f[i] be the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence starting at index i. It can be computed in O(n log n) by scanning the array from right to left and running the tails technique on the negated values (a strictly increasing run read right to left in the original is strictly increasing in the negated values). The longest length is L = max f[i].

Every longest subsequence has the form: element with f = L, then element with f = L-1, and so on down to f = 1. So the choice at each step is limited to indices whose f equals the count of elements still needed, with the usual constraints (later index, larger value than the previous pick). Any such candidate can still be completed to full length L, so greedily taking the smallest value is safe: a smaller value at the earliest position always wins the lexicographic comparison.

Among equal values take the earliest index; it leaves a superset of the continuations of the later one. Bucket indices by their f value, so each step only scans its own bucket and the whole reconstruction is O(n). Total time O(n log n), memory O(n).
